title: Humboldt’s mountain
teaches: Chimborazo, climate zones and why they move

blocks.text: On 23 June 1802 three men climbed the snowfields of Chimborazo, the great volcano of central Ecuador, then believed to be the highest mountain in the world. Alexander von Humboldt was a Prussian nobleman who had spent his inheritance on a scientific expedition to Spanish America; Aimé Bonpland was his French botanist; Carlos Montúfar was a young man from a leading Quito family. They had sent their porters back. They climbed in thin cotton clothes, with altitude sickness, bleeding from the gums, until a ravine in the ice stopped them at about 5,900 metres, by Humboldt's barometer the highest any European had stood.

All the way up Humboldt had been measuring: air pressure, temperature, the boiling point of water, the blueness of the sky. Bonpland had been collecting plants and noting the height at which each grew. At the bottom of the mountain were sugar cane and palms; then forests of tree ferns and evergreen trees hung with moss; then fields of potatoes and barley, and the last scrubby trees; then a wide belt of tussock grass and cushion plants, the **páramo**; then lichens and a few small flowering plants on bare rock, and finally snow.

Back in Europe, Humboldt drew what they had seen as a single picture. Published in 1807, his *Tableau physique des Andes* shows Chimborazo in cross-section, with the names of plants written up its slope at the heights where they grew, and columns on either side listing, for each height, the temperature, air pressure, humidity, the crops farmed there and the animals found. It was one of the first pictures to show nature as a system in which everything varied together with height, and the plants with it[^tableau].

Humboldt saw that the zones on the mountain matched the zones of the whole Earth. Palms and tropical forest at the foot, like the lowlands of the equator. Forests of evergreen trees above, like temperate lands. Then grassland and low shrubs, like the treeless tundra of the far north, and ice at the top like the poles. Climbing a few kilometres up a mountain was like travelling thousands of kilometres toward a pole.

parts.title: A kilometre up, a thousand north

blocks.text: The reason is temperature. Air cools as it rises and expands, so mountain air is colder than lowland air at the same latitude, by about 6.5 °C for every kilometre up on average[^lapse], a rate meteorologists call the **lapse rate**. Travelling toward a pole cools things too, but slowly: at mid-latitudes the yearly average falls by roughly 0.7 °C for every 100 kilometres. So a kilometre of height is worth something like 900 kilometres of travel toward a pole.

Each plant does well within a range of temperatures, with enough water, and plants with similar needs end up in the same places. That makes zones. Their edges are not where the plants were put, but where conditions stop suiting them. Warm the climate, and every limit moves uphill, by about 150 metres for each degree, since 1 ÷ 6.5 is about 0.15 kilometres. Moist air cools more slowly than dry, and on Chimborazo's wet slopes the rate is nearer 5.5 °C per kilometre, so there each degree moves the zones nearer 180 metres.

blocks.caption: Chimborazo's zones of plants, by mean yearly temperature, with temperature falling about 5.5 °C per kilometre up these slopes. Warm or cool the climate and see where the zones go. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then warm the climate by 3 °C

blocks.text: A mountain is a cone, so there is less ground at each step up. When the zones slide up, each one squeezes into a narrower ring, and the highest has nowhere to go. Species of mountaintops are among the first that warming may push off the world, as their zone shrinks to the summit and then past it.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: Air cools about 6.5 °C per kilometre up; at mid-latitudes the yearly average falls about 0.7 °C per 100 kilometres toward the pole. So climbing 1 kilometre cools you as much as going about 6.5 ÷ 0.7 × 100 ≈ 900 kilometres north: from Seattle, roughly to the north end of Vancouver Island and beyond.

parts.title: Two hundred years later, and a correction

blocks.text: In 2012 a team led by Naia Morueta-Holme, a Danish ecologist, climbed Chimborazo with Humboldt's records and searched for the highest plants, comparing the heights where they now grew with the heights on his picture. The upper limit of plant life had moved up by about 500 metres. The glacier that capped the mountain had shrunk back a long way and the climate there had warmed, and plants had followed both up the slope. Their paper, published in 2015, became a famous example of climate change seen through two centuries of records.

Then the record itself was checked. In 2019 the historian and archaeologist Pascal Moret and colleagues went back to Humboldt's and Bonpland's notebooks and found that much of the plant data in the *Tableau* did not come from Chimborazo at all. Some came from Antisana, another volcano, and other places they had passed, drawn together on one mountain for the picture. Using only the observations that really came from the slopes they described, Moret's team concluded that the plants had moved up, but by less than the 2015 paper said.

Both papers matter. Old records are precious because they let us see change over centuries, and they need the same scrutiny as new data, including where exactly each observation was made. The plants' climb is real; how far, for Humboldt's mountain, is still argued over.

The Cascades and Olympics have their own zones. Around Seattle the lowland forest is western hemlock, western red cedar and Douglas fir. Climbing above roughly 700 to 1,000 metres, Pacific silver fir takes over; above about 1,200 metres, mountain hemlock and subalpine fir, with heather meadows in the openings; and higher still, the trees shrink to wind-cut clumps and give way to alpine plants and rock. On the dry east side of the Cascades the zones run the other way at the bottom, with the forest stopping not at the cold top but at the dry foot, where pines give way to sagebrush, as branch S, The dry side, shows.

blocks.title: Outside
points: On the drive up to Hurricane Ridge, Paradise or Snoqualmie Pass, watch for where the trees change: their height, how far apart they stand, the shape of their tops. Note the height of each change from a map or your phone, and compare it with the next mountain you visit.

blocks.text: Across the whole planet, the main types of vegetation, called **biomes**, follow two numbers more than anything else: how warm a place is on average, and how much rain and snow it gets in a year. In 1975 Robert Whittaker, the same ecologist who counted trees in the Smoky Mountains in lesson 15, drew them on one chart. Where it is cold, there is tundra; a little warmer, northern conifer forest. In the middle temperatures, more rain means grassland, then woodland, then broadleaf forest, then temperate rainforest. In the tropics, desert, then savanna, then seasonal forest, then rainforest.

blocks.caption: Biomes by mean yearly temperature and rain, simplified from Whittaker's chart. Pick a place, or move one with the sliders.

blocks.text: Seattle and the Hoh rainforest on the Olympic Peninsula have almost the same temperature; the Hoh gets nearly four times the rain. Ritzville, in the wheat country east of the Cascades (near Harrow, the made-up town of the Clouds course), is barely cooler than Seattle but gets less than a third of its rain, and that makes it grassland, not forest. The chart is a summary, and real boundaries also depend on soil, fire and the timing of rain through the year[^tropics]. But it explains a good deal of the world's vegetation with two numbers.

blocks.caption: Six questions on climate and where things live
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why did Humboldt compare climbing Chimborazo to travelling toward the poles?
choices: Temperature falls with height as it does toward the poles
The mountain's plants had come there from the north
The sun is weaker on mountains near the equator
items.why: Air cools about 6.5 °C per kilometre up, so a few kilometres of height span the same temperatures as thousands of kilometres of latitude.

items.ask: The climate warms by 2 °C on a mountain where the air cools about 6.5 °C per kilometre up. About how far do the plants' zones move?
items.why: 2 ÷ 6.5 is about 0.3 km. Each zone's lower and upper limits move up by about that much.

items.ask: Why are mountaintop species especially at risk from warming?
choices: Their zone narrows as it climbs, then runs out of mountain
They can't set seed in warmer weather
items.why: Each step up has less ground. The highest zone has nowhere higher to go.

items.ask: What did Pascal Moret's team find in 2019 about Humboldt's picture of Chimborazo?
choices: Much of its data came from other places, so the rise was smaller
Humboldt's barometer had overstated every height
The plants had not moved at all
items.why: The Tableau combined observations from several places. Using only those from the slopes, the shift was real but smaller.

items.ask: Seattle and Ritzville, in eastern Washington, have similar yearly temperatures. Why is one forest and the other grassland?
choices: Ritzville gets less than a third of Seattle's rain
Ritzville's soil is too rich for trees
items.why: On Whittaker's chart, at the same temperature, less rain moves a place from forest to grassland.

items.ask: Which two numbers best predict a place's biome?
choices: Its mean yearly temperature and its yearly rain
Its height above the sea and its latitude
Its soil and its distance from the sea
items.why: Height and latitude act through temperature. Temperature and rain together set most of what can grow.

summary: **Humboldt mapped plants up Chimborazo in 1802.** His 1807 picture showed each plant at its height, with temperature and pressure beside it.
**Height and latitude both cool the air.** About 6.5 °C per kilometre up; a kilometre up is worth roughly 900 kilometres toward a pole.
**Zones of plants follow temperature.** Their edges are where conditions stop suiting each species.
**When climate warms, the zones move up.** About 150 metres for each degree, and the highest zone shrinks toward the summit.
**Chimborazo's plants have climbed since 1802.** By how much is argued, since some of Humboldt's data came from other mountains.
**Old records need checking too.** Where and how each observation was made decides what it can show.
**Temperature and rain set the biome.** Whittaker's chart places tundra, forest, grassland, desert and rainforest by those two numbers.

tableau.title: Humboldt's fame
tableau.text: Humboldt was the most famous scientist in the world for much of the nineteenth century. Darwin took his travel books on the Beagle and said they shaped his life. The Humboldt Current, Humboldt penguin, Humboldt squid and Humboldt County in California are all named for him.

tropics.title: Why the tropics hold more species
tropics.text: Tropical forests hold far more kinds of trees, insects and birds than temperate ones. Ecologists still argue over why: more energy and a longer growing season, older and more stable habitats, faster evolution in the warmth, more pests that keep any one tree from becoming common, or all of these at once.

lapse.title: Why rising air cools
lapse.text: Air pressure falls with height. Rising air expands as the pressure on it drops, and expanding gas cools because it does work pushing the surrounding air aside. Dry air cools about 10 °C per kilometre; moist air, which releases heat as its water condenses into cloud, cools less. The average is about 6.5 °C.
